title: Thousands March Down Kyiv's Khreshchatyk Demanding Ousted Defence Minister's Return
excerpt: Protesters flood Ukraine's main boulevard in the largest rally yet against President Zelenskiy's decision to dismiss Mykhailo Fedorov, the tech-savvy reformer credited with transforming the country's wartime military.
body:
• Several thousand Ukrainians marched through Kyiv's Khreshchatyk boulevard on July 31, the largest demonstration since protests erupted over Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov's dismissal in mid-July.
  • Fedorov, 35, has rejected alternative government posts offered by President Zelenskiy, saying they lack the authority needed to continue defence reforms.
  • The crisis has already cost commander-in-chief Oleksandr Syrskyi his position and raised questions about Ukraine's democratic governance during wartime.

Several thousand Ukrainians marched through central Kyiv on Friday, flooding the capital's main thoroughfare Khreshchatyk in the most forceful demonstration yet against President Volodymyr Zelenskiy's decision to oust Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, according to Reuters. The rally signalled that opposition to the poorly explained government reshuffle that began in mid-July remains entrenched.

Fedorov, who took charge of the wartime ministry in January, was dismissed on July 15 in a cabinet shake-up that also removed Prime Minister Yulia Svyrydenko. The 35-year-old former digital transformation minister had been credited with driving technological innovation in the military — particularly Ukraine's drone programme — and leading anti-corruption efforts within the defence sector.

"I don't like it when decisions are made, and then no one can explain why they were made."

— Oleksandr, 40, IT worker in Kyiv

A Crisis That Keeps Escalating

Zelenskiy initially said he removed Fedorov because of an irreparable rift with then commander-in-chief Oleksandr Syrskyi, a Soviet-trained general criticised by some soldiers for a rigid command style and high troop losses. The president said the two could no longer sit at the same table.

https://x.com/KyivPost/status/2083247939787362433

But the explanation failed to satisfy the public. Within days, thousands poured into the streets demanding Fedorov's reinstatement and Syrskyi's removal. Zelenskiy dismissed Syrskyi a week later under public pressure, replacing him with respected field commander Mykhailo Drapatyi. Major General Yevhenii Khmara was appointed acting defence minister.

Speculation has since grown that Fedorov was forced out for his efforts to tackle alleged corruption in defence procurement. In a recent interview, Fedorov appeared to lend weight to those claims, though he offered no specifics. Earlier, at a news conference on July 16, he was blunt: "Decisions are made based on loyalty, not data. There is sabotage of changes."

Zelenskiy offered Fedorov several alternative roles, including vice prime minister for defence innovation. Fedorov publicly rejected them all, saying the posts carried no real authority to pursue reform.

What the Protests Reveal

Friday's march through Kyiv's historic centre carried echoes of protests a year ago, when Zelenskiy attempted to strip Ukraine's anti-corruption agencies of their independence — a move he ultimately reversed. Protest organiser Dmytro Koziatynskyi, a military veteran, told Reuters that Zelenskiy should give Fedorov a year to pursue reforms and judge him on results.

"We don't need Fedorov just as a figurehead. We need Fedorov as a young reformer. The posts offered by the president do not carry sufficient influence or provide the necessary tools to press on with reform."

— Dmytro Koziatynskyi, protest organiser and military veteran

For many demonstrators, the issue extends beyond one minister. Some questioned whether the war against Russia — now in its fifth year — can be won without the technological modernisation of the post-Soviet army that Fedorov embodied. His dismissal came as Ukraine was pressing a deep-strike campaign against Russian military and energy infrastructure, and making gains on the frontline.

Matteo Mecacci, director of the European Policy Institute in Kyiv, said the demonstrations show Ukrainians view the dispute not as an internal government matter but as one directly affecting the war effort and public confidence in institutions. "The way out for Zelenskiy probably cannot be limited to another personnel decision," he said.

What's Next

Zelenskiy has yet to submit a permanent replacement for Fedorov to parliament, which is in summer recess until August 18. Under Ukrainian law, the defence ministry must be headed by a civilian — complicating any effort to formalise Khmara's appointment.

Protesters have declared their campaign open-ended. "We are not in a rush. We are here to stay. We have no choice," said Iryna, a 38-year-old businesswoman. The crowd's chants of "the people are the power" underscored a broader message: that democratic accountability does not pause during wartime.

Western allies are watching closely. A senior European official in Kyiv told CNN the decision to remove Fedorov was "a bit of a shocker" and could have repercussions for Ukraine's relations with key partners, who viewed Fedorov as committed to tackling corruption in both the military and government.
nri_angle: Sustained protests in wartime Ukraine highlight democratic governance under pressure, a dynamic closely watched by global observers including Indian analysts monitoring the war's geopolitical fallout.
